questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain opposite fine particulate trends in two areas

stimulus.body: A translator's footnote records that a monitoring network has reported the same broad pattern for four decades: fine particulate levels fell in the metropolitan core while rising in areas downwind of a new industrial park. The footnote asks the translator to keep the phrase steady downward trend for the core only, since the rural figures do not follow it.

questions.stem: Translator's note 4401 asks which single explanation best accounts for the opposite trends recorded in the core and downwind areas.

options.text: The core reduced its traffic while the industrial park increased heavy vehicle freight
options.misconception: ignores the downwind increase in heavy vehicle activity

options.text: Cleaner vehicle standards cut core emissions while freight traffic near the park added them
The monitoring instruments were recalibrated so that the core readings were lowered
options.misconception: assumes instrument drift explains a real spatial difference

options.text: The core moved to cleaner fuels while the park has no emissions at all to measure
options.misconception: treats an absence of measured emissions as zero emissions

questions.explanation: Opposite trends point to different local sources: lower core traffic emissions and added freight emissions near the park fit the pattern. Instrument drift would affect the whole network, and the park still emits.
questions.hint: Look for a local difference in emissions.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the soil textural class with the smallest particles
questions.stem: A translator's glossary note asks which soil texture class contains the smallest mineral particles and holds the most water for plant growth.

options.text: Sandy soil, whose large particles leave wide spaces that drain freely
options.misconception: confuses the largest particle class with the smallest

options.text: Silty soil, whose medium particles settle into a dense surface crust
options.misconception: attributes a crusting behaviour to the wrong class

options.text: Loamy soil, whose balanced particle mix gives the best nutrient holding
options.misconception: picks a general purpose class for a specific size question

options.text: Clayey soil, whose tiny particles give the highest water holding capacity

questions.explanation: Clay is the smallest particle class, and its fine surface area holds the most water and nutrients. Sand drains freely, silt is intermediate, and loam is a mixture rather than a single size class.
questions.hint: Think about the smallest particle class.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how cation exchange capacity governs lime retention
questions.stem: A translator's explanatory note asks for a clear account of why the exchange capacity of a soil governs how much lime it holds.

answer.exemplar: Cation exchange capacity is the total amount of positively charged ions a soil can hold on the surfaces of its clay and organic particles. Those sites are negatively charged and act as a reservoir, holding calcium, magnesium, potassium, ammonium and hydrogen in exchangeable form so that plant roots can take them up from solution. When the soil is acidic, hydrogen and aluminium occupy most of the sites, so there is less room for calcium and magnesium and the structure weakens. Adding lime supplies calcium and magnesium that displace hydrogen from the exchange sites and restore the base supply.

questions.explanation: The exchange sites hold plant-available ions, so a soil with high capacity buffers change and holds more lime. The item tests the reservoir role of cation exchange rather than total lime content.
questions.hint: Think of the exchange sites as a reservoir.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify contour ploughing and basin tillage in a description

stimulus.body: A translator's margin comment describes a hillside farm where the ploughing lines follow the same height across the slope rather than running straight down it. The comment notes that between the planted rows the farmer leaves shallow basins that catch the water which runs off after heavy rain.

questions.stem: Field margin note 4405 asks which pair of practices the described farm is using.

options.text: Contour ploughing and basin tillage, both of which slow and store runoff
Strip cropping and shelterbelts, both of which use trees to slow the wind
options.misconception: confuses vegetative windbreaks with surface works

options.text: Terracing and flood irrigation, both of which bring water onto the slope
options.misconception: treats irrigation terraces as erosion control

options.text: Deep ploughing and drainage ditches, both of which remove water quickly
options.misconception: misses that runoff must be slowed, not removed

questions.explanation: Contour lines plus basins between rows slow runoff and hold it on the slope: contour farming with basin tillage. Strip cropping mixes crops, terraces reshape slopes, drainage speeds flow.
questions.hint: Ask whether runoff is slowed or removed.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Select the principal benefit of a cover crop
questions.stem: Glossary draft note 4406 asks which benefit of growing a cover crop between cash crops the note should render most carefully.

options.text: Replacing the need for fertiliser because the cover crop supplies all nutrients
options.misconception: overstates the nutrient contribution of a cover crop

options.text: Increasing the total amount of soil water available for the next cash crop
options.misconception: assumes cover crops add water to the soil

options.text: Protecting bare soil from erosion and capturing nitrate between cash crops
Eliminating weeds so that no further weed control is needed in the cash crop
options.misconception: treats weed suppression as complete control

questions.explanation: A cover crop keeps roots and residue across the surface, cutting raindrop impact and taking up nitrate that would leach. It replaces no fertiliser, uses soil water, and does not end weed control.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to bare soil.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how irrigation creates salinity in previously unsalted land
questions.stem: The translator's research note asks for a description of how irrigation can create a salinity problem in land that was not salty before.

answer.exemplar: Irrigation adds water to the soil profile, and where that water evaporates it leaves its dissolved salts behind in the upper layers. Over repeated cycles the salt concentration in the root zone rises, because the water is removed by the leaves while the salts remain and are carried downward only slowly. Where drainage is poor, or where groundwater is shallow and salty, capillary rise can pull more saline water into the root zone. Plants then face both osmotic stress, as water becomes harder to extract, and ion toxicity, and the usual response is to leach salts below the root zone with good drainage, which requires somewhere for the water to go.

questions.explanation: Evaporation leaves salts behind as water is removed, so salts accumulate in the root zone where drainage is poor. The item tests the link between irrigation, evaporation, drainage and salt build-up.
questions.hint: Think about what evaporation leaves behind.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a plateau that follows a long decline

stimulus.body: A translator's note records that annual mean fine particulate concentrations in a large city fell by about forty per cent between 1995 and 2015, then changed very little over the following decade. The note adds that household wood burning in the surrounding hills was measured separately and rose over the same period.

questions.stem: Trend commentary 4409 asks what the flattening trend after the earlier fall most likely indicates.

options.text: Control measures reached their limit, so further gains need new sources of change
The earlier fall was a measurement error, so the whole trend cannot be trusted
options.misconception: dismisses a long measured series on a guess

options.text: Fine particulates are now produced mostly by a source that cannot be controlled
options.misconception: assumes every particulate source is uncontrollable

options.text: The city moved all particulate emissions to the surrounding rural area
options.misconception: invents a relocation not shown by the data

questions.explanation: A fall then a plateau suggests the easy gains were taken and further progress needs new measures. An error would not reproduce a decade of data, and sources remain controllable.
questions.hint: Think about what a plateau in a trend means.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the effect of organic matter on a sandy soil
questions.stem: Pedology note 4410 asks which soil property is most directly improved when a farmer adds plenty of organic matter to a sandy soil.

options.text: The rate at which water drains through the profile to deep drainage
options.misconception: assumes organic matter increases drainage rate

options.text: The speed at which the plough turns the soil in the spring
options.misconception: confuses tilth with the question being asked

options.text: The number of days the soil can be worked without becoming smeared
options.misconception: picks a workability property instead of water retention

options.text: The amount of water the soil can store for plant use between rainfalls

questions.explanation: Organic matter raises the water holding capacity of a coarse soil and slows drainage, so more rain is available to plants. It does not speed drainage, and workability is a separate property.
questions.hint: Think about what sandy soils lack.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain what base saturation indicates about a soil
questions.stem: A translator's note asks for an explanation of how base saturation indicates whether a soil's exchange sites are in good condition.

answer.exemplar: Base saturation is the proportion of the soil's exchange sites occupied by base cations such as calcium, magnesium and potassium rather than by hydrogen or aluminium. A soil with high base saturation has most of its remaining nutrient supply stored in forms that plants can take up directly, and its structure is firmer because calcium bridges clay particles together. A low base saturation means the sites are occupied by hydrogen and exchangeable aluminium, which also drives the soil acid. Tracking the percentage over time shows whether liming has worked, because a single test of pH alone does not reveal how much of the capacity is held by bases.

questions.explanation: Base saturation is the share of exchange sites held by bases rather than acid cations. High base saturation means nutrients are plant-available and structure is firmer, and it shows whether liming worked.
questions.hint: Think about what sits on the exchange sites.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how bunds and terrace drains retain sediment

stimulus.body: A translator's footnote describes a hillside where bunds have been built along the contour lines and where the runoff from each storm is captured in the terrace drains instead of running down the slope. The footnote notes that silt accumulating behind the bunds is dug out each year and spread over the field.

questions.stem: Terrace footnote 4413 asks which outcome of the described system the translator should render most accurately.

options.text: Gully erosion spreading downhill, because the drains follow the steepest line
options.misconception: misreads the layout as accelerating runoff

options.text: Sheet erosion removing the whole topsoil layer every season
options.misconception: confuses the retained silt with sheet erosion

options.text: Runoff being detained so that sediment is deposited and kept on the slope
Salts accumulating on the surface because drainage water cannot leave the field
options.misconception: treats detained water as a salinity process

questions.explanation: Bunds and terrace drains detain runoff, so the sediment settles behind them and is returned to the field rather than carried downslope. Drains follow the contour, not the steepest line, and detained water does not create salinity.
questions.hint: Focus on where the water and its sediment end up.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the main consequence of leaving soil bare over winter
questions.stem: Winter cover entry 4414 asks which of the following is the most likely consequence of leaving soil bare over winter.

options.text: Reduced loss of nitrate because bare soil is cool and dry in early spring
options.misconception: believes bare soil protects nutrients

options.text: Greater loss of nitrate by leaching and increased risk of soil erosion
Increased biological activity because bare soil receives more sunlight
options.misconception: confuses sunlight with biological activity

options.text: Higher soil temperature and therefore faster decomposition of organic matter
options.misconception: reverses the thermal effect of bare soil

questions.explanation: Bare soil is exposed to rain that carries nitrate below the root zone and to wind and water that remove particles. Cold bare soil has less biological activity and cools the profile.
questions.hint: Consider what rain and wind do to bare soil.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why salt-tolerant plants do not remove salinity
questions.stem: Marginal gloss 4415 asks for a plain explanation of why salt-tolerant plants help on a saline field but do not remove the salinity problem.

answer.exemplar: Salt-tolerant species cope with saline soil by adjusting the osmotic potential inside their cells, so they can take up water even when the soil solution is salty, and by limiting the uptake of damaging ions or storing them in old leaves that are shed. That protects the plant but does not change the soil. The salt stays in the profile, so without a way to remove it the field remains saline and the yield advantage of a tolerant crop is a small margin over an intolerant one, while the underlying cause, poor drainage or excessive irrigation, is untouched.

questions.explanation: Tolerance mechanisms protect the plant rather than the soil, so salts remain in the root zone. The item tests the difference between managing a crop symptom and correcting the underlying salinity.
questions.hint: Think about whether the salt leaves the soil.

questions.learningObjective: Explain a plateau that coincides with the closure of a point source

stimulus.body: A translator's note describes a regional monitoring programme that has reported annual mean fine particulate concentrations at a suburban site since 1990. The series falls steeply until about 2005 and then flattens, and the note records that industrial emissions from one plant were closed in 2004 while traffic on the ring road has grown steadily every year since.

questions.stem: Network footnote 4417 asks which explanation best fits a decline that stops in the year a major point source closed.

options.text: The closed plant was the only source of fine particles in the area
options.misconception: ignores the growing traffic source

options.text: The monitoring instrument drifted after 2005 and produced false readings
options.misconception: assumes instrument drift without evidence

options.text: The plant closure removed one source while traffic growth replaced it
Fine particulate formation stopped in 2005 because of a change in regional climate
options.misconception: invents a climate step change with no data

questions.explanation: The timing matches source substitution: closing one emitter lowered concentrations until traffic growth added them back. An instrument fault would not coincide with a closure, and no climate step occurred.
questions.hint: Match the timing of the change to the sources.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the soil horizon turned by a mouldboard plough
questions.stem: Profile gloss 4418 asks which soil horizon the plough mixes and that a translator should describe as the layer turned by a mouldboard plough.

options.text: The topsoil, the dark surface horizon that is rich in organic matter
The subsoil, the pale layer beneath that contains little organic matter
options.misconception: confuses the ploughed layer with the layer below

options.text: The parent material, the weathered rock that forms the base of the profile
options.misconception: identifies the deepest horizon as the plough layer

options.text: The bedrock layer, the unweathered rock beneath the whole soil profile
options.misconception: mistakes bedrock for a soil horizon

questions.explanation: A mouldboard plough turns the topsoil, the dark organic-rich surface horizon supporting most root activity. The subsoil and parent material lie beneath and are disturbed only by deeper tillage.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why leaching is worse on sandy soils than on clays
questions.stem: Drainage gloss 4419 asks for an explanation of why leaching is a problem on sandy soils but less so on heavy clays.

answer.exemplar: Leaching occurs when water that has drained through the root zone carries dissolved ions away with it. On a sandy soil the particles are large, the pores are wide and the water moves quickly, so there is little time for the exchange sites to hold the calcium and magnesium that roots need. The same water carries nitrate with it, so the soil is left both less fertile and more acidic. On a heavy clay the pores are small, the water moves slowly and the large exchange capacity of clay holds cations for much longer, so the same rainfall produces far less loss, which is why clays are commonly used to build up fertility over time.

questions.explanation: Fast drainage on sandy soil allows little time for exchange sites to retain bases, so leaching removes nutrients. Slow drainage and high exchange capacity on clay reduce the same loss.
questions.hint: Think about how fast the water moves.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the element that stops runoff becoming a fast flow

stimulus.body: A translator's note describes a terraced hillside where each level has a level planted row, a grassed strip along the contour and a bund at the outer edge. The note records that infiltration basins between the planted row and the grassed strip are emptied after each heavy storm.

questions.stem: Terrace gloss 4421 asks which single element of the described system does the most to stop water reaching the field as a fast flow.

options.text: The level planted row, because a level row cannot generate any runoff at all
options.misconception: treats a level row as eliminating runoff entirely

options.text: The bund at the outer edge, because it blocks and detains the flow
The grassed strip along the contour, because grass slows water better than any earth bank
options.misconception: claims grass out-performs a bund as a barrier

options.text: The infiltration basins, because they store the whole storm without overflowing
options.misconception: assumes basins never need emptying

questions.explanation: The bund at the outer edge is the barrier that stops a sheet of water becoming a fast downslope flow. The level row and grass slow and spread the water, while basins store only part of a storm.
questions.hint: Look for the physical barrier in the sequence.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Select a cover crop suited to capturing residual nitrate
questions.stem: Species list 4422 asks which cover crop species is best suited to the stated purpose of capturing nitrate left in the soil after a harvest.

options.text: A cereal rye crop, because its deep fibrous roots scour the soil surface
options.misconception: links a deep root crop with nitrate capture in the wrong way

options.text: A phacelia crop, because its flowers attract pollinators into the field
options.misconception: judges a cover crop by wildlife value alone

options.text: A vetch and clover mixture, because legumes fix nitrogen for the next crop
options.misconception: confuses nitrogen fixation with nitrate capture

options.text: A deep-rooted legume, because it takes up residual nitrate and adds nitrogen

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a salt crust indicates upward salt movement
questions.stem: Crust description 4423 explains how a salt crust on the soil surface is used to diagnose a salinity problem.

answer.exemplar: A white crust on the surface forms when saline groundwater or irrigation water rises through the profile by capillary action and the water then evaporates, leaving the dissolved salts behind as the soil dries. Because the salt appears at the surface, the crust is a visible marker of salt movement upward, and it usually appears in patches where the water table is shallow or the surface crust is strongest. Seeing the crust is a prompt to test both the soil and the shallow groundwater for electrical conductivity, since a surface crust alone does not reveal how deep the problem extends through the profile.

questions.explanation: Surface crusts form when saline water rises and evaporates, leaving salt behind, so they mark upward salt movement. The item tests the use of a visible sign to prompt measurement.
questions.hint: Think about where the salt came from.

questions.learningObjective: Match a gritty feel to the correct particle class
questions.stem: Textural gloss 4426 asks which particle size class the note should use for the material that feels gritty between the fingers.

options.text: Sand, the largest class, made of separate grains visible to the eye
Silt, the middle class, which feels smooth and floury when dry
options.misconception: confuses the smooth feel of silt with grittiness

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how exchangeable aluminium harms acid soils
questions.stem: Root damage gloss 4427 asks for an explanation of why aluminium becomes a problem on acid soils even before obvious signs of damage appear.

answer.exemplar: As soil pH falls, the hydrogen ions on the exchange sites become more numerous and aluminium is released from the clay and organic fractions into the soil solution. Aluminium is not a nutrient; at low concentrations it inhibits root elongation and root hairs, so the plant cannot explore as much of the profile for water and nutrients. It also interferes with the uptake of calcium, magnesium and phosphate, and it can be toxic to the root tips directly. The practical consequence is that a crop may show a nutrient shortage that adding more of that nutrient will not fix, because the problem is the aluminium blocking the uptake in the first place.

questions.explanation: Acid soils release exchangeable aluminium, which inhibits root growth and blocks uptake of other nutrients. The item tests why a deficiency symptom may not respond to adding more of the missing nutrient.
questions.hint: Think about what aluminium does to roots.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate an area-weighted average soil loss rate
questions.stem: Catchment arithmetic 4428 gives a catchment where 60 per cent of the land is gently sloping and 40 per cent is steep, and where gentle slopes lose 2 tonnes per hectare per year while steep slopes lose 10 tonnes per hectare per year; what is the average loss across the catchment in tonnes per hectare per year?
questions.explanation: Weight each rate by its share: 0.6 times 2 is 1.2 and 0.4 times 10 is 4, adding to 5.2 tonnes per hectare per year. A plain average would treat the slopes as equally common.
questions.hint: Weight each rate by its share of the land.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why contoured fields retain soil after storms

One was ploughed along the contour line, the other up and down the slope, and both were planted with the same crop in the same season. questions.stem: Interval note 4430 asks which of the following is the main way a cover crop reduces the amount of soil organic matter lost from a field.

options.text: By raising the soil temperature so that decomposition is faster each spring
options.misconception: reverses the effect of a cover on soil temperature

options.text: By keeping living roots and residues at the surface that feed soil organisms
By absorbing rainfall so that less water reaches the soil surface at all
options.misconception: confuses interception with soil protection

options.text: By raising the pH of the soil so that organic matter breaks down more slowly
options.misconception: assumes a cover crop is mainly a liming material

questions.explanation: Living roots feed soil organisms and residues become organic matter, so carbon inputs continue while covered. A cover does not heat the soil, block all rainfall or act as a lime.
questions.hint: Think about carbon inputs and soil life.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why saline damage appears after years of irrigation
questions.stem: Irrigation history 4431 explains why salt damage in an irrigated district often appears worst where drainage was once thought to be adequate.

answer.exemplar: Drainage is judged by the rate at which water moves through the soil, but the rate of movement is not the only thing that matters. As irrigation continues, the salts that were once washed down accumulate below the root zone, and the water table rises because the applied irrigation water has to go somewhere. Once the water table is close to the surface, saline water is drawn upward by capillary rise and by the pumping of the roots, and it evaporates at the surface, depositing salt in the zone the crop is trying to use. The land that looks well drained in a single wet year can therefore be the land that fails after a decade of irrigation, because the salt has been stored below rather than removed.

questions.explanation: Repeated irrigation stores salt below the root zone and raises the water table, so saline water returns to the surface later. The item tests why short-term drainage checks can mislead.
questions.hint: Think about where the salt goes after each irrigation.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpret diverging indoor and outdoor particulate trends

stimulus.body: A translator's note records that in a region with rising household incomes, the concentration of fine particulate measured inside homes fell steadily over fifteen years while the outdoor concentration stayed flat. The note adds that cooking indoors shifted from open fires and solid fuel to cleaner gas and electricity.

questions.stem: Indoor outdoor gloss 4433 asks what the divergence between indoor and outdoor fine particulate suggests.

options.text: A change in indoor sources has been removed from the outdoor total
The outdoor monitors have been recalibrated to report a rising trend
options.misconception: assumes an instrument change caused the outdoor pattern

options.text: Indoor particles are simply settling out of the outdoor air in the street
options.misconception: treats indoor and outdoor air as one shared reservoir

options.text: Fine particles cannot pass between indoors and outdoors through windows
options.misconception: assumes buildings are sealed against outdoor particles

questions.explanation: Indoor and outdoor trends move separately because indoor sources changed, so cleaner fuels explain falling indoor levels while traffic keeps the outdoor total flat. Buildings exchange air, so the two stay linked.
questions.hint: Compare which sources each measurement includes.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why sandy soil holds water for only a short time
questions.stem: Permeability note 4434 asks which of the following best explains why a sandy soil can hold water for only a short time after heavy rain.

options.text: The sand particles have a large total surface area that soaks up the water
options.misconception: reverses the relationship between surface area and drainage

options.text: The sandy soil has almost no organic matter so nothing binds the water
options.misconception: puts the cause in organic matter alone

options.text: The large pores between sand grains let the water drain away quickly
The sandy soil has a high clay content that pushes the water to the surface
options.misconception: assigns a clay property to a sandy soil

questions.explanation: Sand grains are large, so the pores between them are wide and water passes through quickly to deep drainage. Clay has the opposite structure, with fine particles and small pores that hold water against gravity.
questions.hint: Think about pore size between the particles.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why clay holds more exchangeable cations than sand
questions.stem: Weathering gloss 4435 asks for an explanation of why the exchange capacity of a soil is usually higher in a deep, well-weathered clay than in a fresh sandy deposit.

answer.exemplar: Exchange capacity depends on the surface area of the particles that carry the charge. Clay particles are minute, so a kilogram of clay has an enormous surface area compared with a kilogram of sand, and each of those surfaces can hold a layer of exchangeable cations. Organic matter adds more charged surface than the mineral fraction alone, so a topsoil rich in humus can have a high capacity even over sandy material. Weathering also breaks minerals down into finer, more reactive particles with more charge, which is why a mature clay subsoil holds far more of the plant-available nutrients that leaching would otherwise carry away.

questions.explanation: Clay and organic matter offer far more charged surface per unit mass than sand, so they retain more exchangeable cations. The item tests what actually determines exchange capacity.
questions.hint: Think about surface area rather than weight.

questions.stem: Rill measurements 4436 give a rill that is 200 metres long, 0.4 metres wide and 0.3 metres deep; what is the volume of soil in the rill in cubic metres?
questions.explanation: Treat the rill as a prism: length times width times depth gives 200 times 0.4 times 0.3, which equals 24 cubic metres. Rill volumes are often measured this way to size the repair work.

questions.learningObjective: State the general principle behind contour practice

stimulus.body: A translator's note records that a farmer noticed rills beginning below a small rise in the field where rainwater collected and flowed over a short distance. The note records that the farmer then laid the field furrows at right angles to that path and that the rills stopped forming at the same place the following season.

questions.stem: Flow note 4437 asks which general principle of contour practice the note illustrates.

options.text: Terracing, because the rise must be flattened before any other work is done
options.misconception: claims the note describes terrace construction

options.text: Strip cropping, because alternating crops stop water moving across the slope
options.misconception: confuses the principle with alternating crop strips

options.text: Underground drainage, because surface measures cannot reduce the flow of water
options.misconception: assumes subsurface works are required for the effect

options.text: Furrows should run across the slope, perpendicular to the main flow path

questions.explanation: Furrows should run across the slope against the direction water takes, so flow is intercepted and spread rather than concentrated. The note describes contour ploughing, not terracing or strip cropping.
questions.hint: Think about the angle between the furrow and the flow.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why cover crops are grown between cash crops
questions.stem: Interval gloss 4438 asks which of the following is the main reason farmers grow cover crops in the interval between two cash crops rather than leaving the field empty.

options.text: To raise the total nitrogen applied to the field beyond the crop's needs
options.misconception: assumes cover crops add large amounts of nitrogen

options.text: To keep the soil covered and biologically active between the main crops
To break up the compacted layer created by the machinery of the harvest
options.misconception: treats cover cropping as a deep tillage operation

options.text: To make the field look more productive to buyers inspecting the farm
options.misconception: gives cover cropping an ornamental purpose

questions.explanation: A cover crop protects the surface, feeds soil organisms and takes up nutrients during the gap, keeping the field alive rather than bare. It adds little nitrogen and does not replace subsoiling or tidiness.
questions.hint: Think about what happens during the bare interval.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish salinity damage from waterlogging damage
questions.stem: Symptom table 4439 asks for a comparison of the conditions under which salinity and waterlogging damage a soil.

answer.exemplar: Waterlogging and salinity produce different signatures and need different remedies. When a soil is waterlogged, the pore space fills and oxygen cannot reach the roots, so the damage is to the plant rather than to the chemistry, and the cure is to remove the water by improving drainage or by pumping. Salinity acts through the chemistry of the soil solution: water becomes harder to extract because of dissolved salts, and specific ions such as sodium and chlorine injure the roots directly, so the cure is to move the salt out of the root zone by leaching with good drainage. A salt crust on the surface, a rising water table and a decline in the plants together point to salinity, while a permanently wet surface and a smell of sulphide point to waterlogging.

questions.explanation: Waterlogging suffocates roots and is cured by removing water, while salinity changes soil chemistry and is cured by leaching salts away. The item tests separating the two damage mechanisms.
questions.hint: Decide whether the problem is oxygen or chemistry.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a model comparison of emissions drivers

stimulus.body: A translator's note describes an analysis in which a model reproduced the historical record of fine particulate levels in a city when given only the changes in road traffic, coal use and industrial output over the same period. questions.stem: Model footnote 4441 asks what the model comparison supports about the causes of the trend.

options.text: Specific emission sources explain the trend better than population alone
Population growth was the only variable that mattered in the city
options.misconception: ignores the better fit of the source based model

options.text: The model proves that the trend will continue at the same rate
options.misconception: mistakes a historical fit for a forecast

options.text: Air quality has improved only by chance and none of the sources matter
options.misconception: dismisses the evidence of the model fit

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain contrasting drainage in clay and sandy soils
questions.stem: Structure gloss 4442 asks which of the following best explains why a clay soil is described as having poor drainage and a sandy soil as free draining.

options.text: Clay particles are larger than sand particles, so water moves through them slowly
options.misconception: reverses the particle size order

options.text: Sand contains more organic matter, so it holds less of the water it receives
options.misconception: confuses organic matter with drainage behaviour

options.text: Clay has small particles and small pores, so water moves through it slowly
Sand is denser when wet, which pushes water upward to the soil surface
options.misconception: invents an upward flow mechanism for sand

questions.explanation: Clay has the smallest particles, so its pores are tiny and water moves through slowly, keeping the surface wet. Sand has large pores that drain freely, and clay is neither denser nor richer in organic matter.
questions.hint: Think about pore size, not particle weight.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain what cation exchange is in plain terms
questions.stem: Definition box 4443 explains what cation exchange actually is, suitable for a general reader.

answer.exemplar: The surfaces of clay and organic particles carry a negative charge, which attracts positively charged ions in the soil water and holds them loosely on the outside of the particle. Calcium, magnesium, potassium, ammonium and hydrogen can all be held this way, and any one of them can be swapped for another in a reversible exchange. Because the ions are held rather than dissolved, they are not washed away at the first rain and are available to roots when the plant releases hydrogen ions in exchange for nutrients. That reversible holding and swapping is what cation exchange means, and it is why the fertility of a soil depends on what occupies its exchange sites.

questions.explanation: Negatively charged surfaces hold cations loosely and reversibly, which keeps nutrients available and resists leaching. The item tests the basic mechanism rather than its measurement.
questions.hint: Think of the ions as swapping places.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the practices described in a contour strip note

options.misconception: confuses wind control with water erosion control

options.misconception: suggests fallowing a field the note says stays covered

options.text: Contour ploughing, a grassed buffer strip and permanent cover over winter

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Describe the sequence by which a cover crop reduces nitrate loss
questions.stem: Nitrogen sequence 4446 asks which sequence correctly describes how a cover crop reduces nitrate loss to groundwater.

options.text: Roots take up nitrate, the plant is grazed or cut, and the residue is returned to the soil
The soil is covered, so rain cannot reach the nitrate already in the soil
options.misconception: confuses surface protection with nitrogen uptake

options.text: Nitrifying bacteria in the cover crop convert nitrate into a gas that leaves the soil
options.misconception: confuses denitrification with plant uptake

options.text: The cover crop changes the pH so that nitrate is held more tightly on the clay
options.misconception: invents a pH mechanism for nitrate retention

questions.explanation: Cover crop roots take nitrate into the plant, and returning the cut biomass recycles that nitrogen for the next crop. Covering soil does not block rain, and nitrate is not held on clay.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish salt tolerance from salt avoidance in plants
questions.stem: Strategy contrast 4447 explains why salt tolerance and salt avoidance are different strategies in plants.

answer.exemplar: Salt avoidance means keeping the salt out: the plant restricts the uptake of sodium and chloride in the roots, tolerates the osmotic stress of saline soil by adjusting the concentration of its own cell contents, and often isolates the salt in a vacuole or sheds it in old leaves. Salt tolerance means coping with the salt that has already entered, by compartmentalising it away from sensitive parts of the cell or by changing the chemistry of the leaf so that the excess ions can be excreted. The distinction matters because a tolerant species can survive and yield on saline land where an intolerant species simply dies, but neither strategy removes the salt, so the underlying salinity still needs correcting.

questions.explanation: Avoidance keeps salt out of the plant while tolerance copes with salt already inside it. The item tests the distinction between the two strategies and their shared limitation.
questions.hint: Think about whether the salt is excluded or handled.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why one policy produced different trends nearby

stimulus.body: A translator's note records that in one district fine particulate fell steadily after a ban on open burning, and in a neighbouring district with the same ban the concentration did not change because the burning continued from farmland outside the district boundary and drifted across.

options.misconception: misses that the ban covered both districts

options.text: The first district has better monitors, so its readings are more reliable
options.misconception: rejects the second district data without evidence

options.text: Transported smoke from outside the second district kept its concentrations high

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the textural class of a balanced soil
questions.stem: Class gloss 4450 asks which soil textural class the note should use for a soil with roughly equal proportions of sand, silt and clay.

options.text: Loam, a balanced mixture of the three particle classes
Clay, which dominates the structure whenever any clay is present
options.misconception: assumes the smallest fraction defines the class

options.text: Silt, which forms whenever sand and clay are present in equal measure
options.misconception: invents a rule that produces silt from a balanced mix

options.text: Sand, because sand particles separate when the soil is worked while wet
options.misconception: confuses the field feel test with texture classes

questions.explanation: A soil with roughly equal sand, silt and clay is a loam, the general purpose class with good structure and water holding. No single fraction defines the class, and the field feel test is a different method.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why lime recommendations use exchangeable acidity
questions.stem: Lime recommendation 4451 explains why lime recommendations on a soil test rest on exchangeable acidity rather than on pH alone.

answer.exemplar: A pH value tells you how acid the soil water is at the moment of sampling, but it does not tell you how many hydrogen ions are held on the exchange sites waiting to be replaced. Exchangeable acidity measures that reserve directly, by displacing the held hydrogen with a neutral salt and titrating what comes off, so it estimates the reserve of acidity that must be neutralised. A heavily buffered clay can show a moderate pH and still hold a large reserve, so a pH-only recommendation would under-lime it, while a sandy soil with little reserve can show a low pH and need only a small dressing. The reserve also takes time to build, which is why liming decisions are revisited rather than made once.

questions.explanation: pH measures the current solution while exchangeable acidity measures the stored reserve that lime must replace. The item tests why the reserve, not the reading alone, drives the recommendation.
questions.hint: Think about stored versus measured acidity.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a cover crop reduces sediment loss

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of salt tolerance for food production
questions.stem: Food production note 4455 explains why salt tolerance in plants is of limited use on land that must also produce food for people.

answer.exemplar: Salt-tolerant plants survive where salt-tolerant crops cannot, so they are valuable for revegetating saline land and for providing grazing and fuel while the soil is being repaired. For food production the limits are nutritional and economic: many of the most tolerant species are pasture grasses, shrubs or trees with low edible yield, and where a crop can be grown its yield under salinity is often well below the yield of the same crop on normal soil. Toleration also costs the plant, since maintaining a low internal salt concentration or compartmentalising excess ions uses energy that would otherwise go into growth, which is why salt-tolerant varieties are used alongside soil management rather than instead of it.

questions.explanation: Tolerance lets plants survive and revegetate saline land but often costs yield and does not remove the salinity. The item tests why tolerant species supplement soil management rather than replace it.
questions.hint: Think about what the plant spends its energy on.

questions.learningObjective: Match a blocky and sticky feel to the soil class

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why base depletion is a slow form of soil decline
questions.stem: Depletion note 4459 explains why the loss of exchangeable bases is often described as a slow form of soil depletion.

answer.exemplar: The exchange sites hold the plant-available nutrients that the crop removes and that rainwater would otherwise wash away. Each harvest takes some of that reserve, and each leaching event takes a little more, while fresh cations arrive only from weathering, fertiliser, manure or irrigation water. Because the reserve is finite, a field cropped repeatedly without replacement slowly loses the bases that hold the soil together and that the plants need, and the soil becomes more acid as hydrogen and aluminium take the empty sites. The depletion is slow, often measurable only over decades, and it is masked while yields hold up because the reserve is still being drawn down.

questions.explanation: Harvesting and leaching draw on a finite store of exchangeable bases replaced only slowly. The item tests why the loss is gradual and can hide while yields continue.
questions.hint: Think about a reserve that is drawn down.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the gully share of total erosion loss
questions.stem: Erosion split 4460 gives a slope where gully erosion removed 2500 tonnes of soil while sheet erosion removed 375 tonnes over the same period; what percentage of the total loss was caused by gullies?
questions.explanation: The combined loss is 2500 plus 375, which is 2875 tonnes, and 2500 divided by 2875 gives about 0.87, so roughly 87 per cent. Concentrated flow makes gullies dominate the total loss.
questions.hint: Find the total loss, then take the share.
